label: Review of Calculus
notes: This appendix is the analytic toolbox the rest of the book leans on. Across printed pages 642 to 662, Lee collects total derivatives, the chain rule, smoothness, and the inverse and implicit function theorems. Treat it not as facts to memorize but as the local Euclidean machinery that every chart argument later repackages.

label: Total Derivative
notes: The total derivative is defined by an approximation quality, not a formula. A linear map qualifies as the derivative exactly when the leftover error shrinks faster than the displacement. Stress the quotient norm-R over norm-v tending to zero; that vanishing-faster-than-linear condition is what makes the tangent plane the best affine model.

label: Jacobian Matrix
notes: Once differentiability is granted, the abstract linear map becomes a concrete matrix of partial derivatives. Emphasize that partials existing is weaker than differentiability; you need them continuous. The Jacobian is the coordinate representation of the differential, and this is the bridge between hand computation and the intrinsic objects on a manifold.

label: Chain Rule
notes: The chain rule is the statement that linearization respects composition. Linearize F at the point, linearize G at the image, and multiply the Jacobians in that order. I like to call this functoriality. It is why differentials compose cleanly and why coordinate changes on manifolds behave predictably under the tangent map.

label: Smoothness and Mixed Partials
notes: Define the C-k hierarchy and smooth as infinitely differentiable. The headline theorem is equality of mixed partials under a C-two hypothesis. Warn students that the hypothesis is real: there is a classic function whose two mixed partials at the origin disagree because continuity fails. Order of differentiation only commutes when you have earned it.

label: Directional Derivatives
notes: The directional derivative collapses to the differential applied to a vector, which in Euclidean coordinates is the gradient dotted with the direction. Point out that the direction vector need not be a unit vector here; scaling the vector scales the derivative linearly. This linearity in the direction is exactly the content of having a total derivative.

label: Taylor's Theorem
notes: Taylor's theorem is a control statement: subtract the degree-k polynomial and the remainder is governed by order k-plus-one derivatives. The integral form of the remainder is the cleanest for our purposes because it is exact and bounds cleanly. This is the engine behind smooth bump functions and local normal-form arguments later in the book.

label: Differentiation Under the Integral
notes: Differentiating under an integral sign is a licensed interchange of limit and integral. The license is continuity of the parameter partial derivative. I frame this as one member of a family of interchange theorems, alongside uniform convergence results, where the recurring moral is that you may swap two limit operations only when something is uniformly controlled.

label: Inverse Function Theorem
notes: This is the centerpiece. If the total derivative at a point is invertible, the map is a diffeomorphism on some neighborhood. Stress the word local: invertibility of the derivative at one point gives nothing global and no universal radius. The grid picture, a coordinate mesh sent invertibly to a curvilinear mesh, is the mental image to carry forward.

label: Implicit Function Theorem
notes: The implicit function theorem is the level-set face of the same coin. If the block partial in the hidden variable is invertible, the equation F of x and y equals zero solves for y as a smooth function of x near the point. This is precisely how level sets become graphs, and how regular level sets become embedded submanifolds.

label: Contraction Mapping
notes: Both theorems are proved by one engine: the contraction mapping principle. A map that shrinks distances by a fixed factor on a complete space has a unique fixed point, found by iteration. Normalize the derivative to the identity, write inversion as a fixed-point problem, and the contraction supplies both existence and smooth dependence.

label: Synthesis
notes: Pull the threads together. The total derivative is the best linear model, the Jacobian is its matrix, the chain rule composes them, smoothness controls interchanges, and the inverse and implicit theorems convert derivative nonsingularity into local coordinates. Every later manifold construction, charts, slices, submanifolds, normal forms, is this Euclidean fact transported through charts.
